paragraphs.text:
1. The man to be adopted after three sons were disowned.
A rich man disowned three sons; he asks a poor man for his only son in adoption. The poor man is willing to give him; when the son refuses to go, the father disowns him. The son speaks against it.

I never thought it would come about that either my father would hate his children or a rich man would covet them. Long I was in doubt: was the one trying out a friend, or the other a son? Are we then so poor, who have something rich men ask for? If he disowned them undeservedly, I hate a father who casts out so many innocent sons; if deservedly, I hate a house that makes so many guilty. I love poverty equally with my father; I am accustomed to both. Your house is not propped up by many children — though even so you ought not to have given me away; for he is safer against fortune who has something left after his loss. "I disown you," he says; it is plain where you come from. There is but one dispute between us: he thinks me worthy of a fortunate father, I think myself worthy of my own. "I want you to be rich," he says. O I deserve to be disowned, if I leave such a father behind! What you would have me seem I do not know: innocent? but I am disowned; guilty? but I am adopted. Not, as in other disownings, is it in my power not to be disowned: I shall lose my father if I am disowned, and lose him if I am not disowned. What difference is there whether I am cast out or transferred? Although a father is to be obeyed in all things, in this he is not to be obeyed — in that by which he ceases to be a father. It is hard to be without an only son; harder to be without the one whom another covets. The unknown herds of slaves do not delight their master, nor the sounding workhouses of a broad estate: I love my father for nothing. I must needs fear a house unlucky in its children. No fitter time for reconciliation can be found: the rich man is looking for sons.

The other side. Among the rest of poverty's drawbacks this too is great: that a son does not fear being disowned. Wealth raises a man to senatorial rank; wealth marks off the Roman knight from the commons; wealth promotes a man's rank in the camp; by wealth a juror is chosen in the forum. It is easier to praise poverty than to bear it. "If my sons are reformed," he says, "I shall have this one along with them; if they persist, I shall have him in their place."

Outside. Dry declaimers keep more faithfully to the colours they have proposed; for no sweetness of some epigram steals in upon them, no figure tempts them aside. So women who are plain are often chaste: it is not the will they lack, but the corrupter. Gallus Vibius was once a man of as great eloquence as he afterwards was of madness; and he is the only man I know to whom it happened that he came to madness not by chance but by deliberate choice; for while he imitated madmen, while he took frenzy for a charm of talent, what he was feigning he reduced to fact. Otho Junius the father published four books of colours, which our friend Gallio neatly calls the books of Antiphon: so much of dreams is there in them. Syriacus, against Maximus Stertinius, by whom he was being pressed hard, though he had been his companion, said: "For fifteen years I was in your service; tell me what wrong I have done. But this is your way: you call the end of servitude an injury."

2. The oath of husband and wife.
A husband and wife swore that, if anything happened to one of them, the other would die. The husband went abroad; he sent a messenger to his wife to say that he had died. The wife threw herself down. Revived, she is ordered by her father to leave her husband; she will not. She is disowned. She speaks against it.

Immortal gods, with what wisdom you owe and you rule the human race: you brought it about that this should be not a danger to one who loved, but a test. Does my father-in-law wish to part those whom not even death will part? "I will die," she says; "I have both cause and example: some women have flung themselves into the burning pyres of their husbands, some have bought their husbands' safety with their own lives. By a brief anxiety this girl is counted, alive, among these." There were constant rivalries: "I cannot live without you" — "no, rather, I cannot live without you"; and as such contests usually end, we swore an oath. This without doubt was the mind of those who swore: that they should not be parted in life, since they took precaution even for this — that they should not be divided by death.

The other side. "I cannot," she says, "leave my husband." Can she not do anything, who can die? She had hardly sent the message of a false death when she received the message of a true one. You can bear to be without your husband; you have borne his journey abroad. You have already been freed of your oath by the latest chance.

Outside. Ovid Naso declaimed this controversia in the school of Arellius Fuscus, his teacher; for he was an admirer of Latro. Latro in a certain preface had said: "Do you not see how a torch, when unmoved, grows dull, and recovers its fire when shaken? Leisure softens men; iron contracts rust through lying idle." Naso said:
"I myself have seen flames grow when the torch was shaken,
and again die when no one stirred them."
This man too said: "The whole labour lies in this — that you grant a wife to love her husband and a husband to love his wife. Then you must needs permit them to swear, if you have permitted them to love." By the same man: "You know few of my faults, father: we have quarrelled at times, and have fallen, and — what perhaps you do not think — we have sworn falsely." Asked once by his friends to strike out three lines, he in turn asked that three be excepted, over which they should have no power. They had written in secret the lines they wanted struck out, he the ones he wanted kept safe: in both sets of tablets the same lines were found, of which, the story goes, the first was — Albinovanus Pedo had been among the arbiters —
"the half-bull man and the half-man bull";
the second:
"and the chill North Wind and the unchill South."
From which it appears that this man of the highest talent lacked not judgement to restrain the licence of his verses, but the will. He used to say that a face was sometimes more becoming for having some mole upon it.

3. The ravisher who does not win over the father.
Let a ravisher, unless within thirty days he has won over both his own father and the father of the ravished woman, perish. A ravisher won over the ravished woman's father; he does not win over his own. He prosecutes him for madness.

Why do you tremble, old age? Why, tongue, do you falter? Why have you gone numb, my eyes? It is not yet the thirtieth day. Not even with a sadder face did he take his daughter's chastity stormed away from her. He was won over too quickly. Not to trace all his vices back to boyhood: he ravished a virgin; he prosecutes his father — all this within thirty days. Do you think I shall promise to an accuser what I refused to a son? Do you wonder that a father hesitates? The law itself hesitates between death and marriage. He has always believed that everything was permitted him; he has never asked anything of me. "He pardoned the man," you say. So was anyone asked before me? I am mad, you see; doubtless I live disgracefully, I know nothing of the law, I do not count your days. "You are mad," you say. Can anyone pardon a man who asks like this? "I will deliberate with my friends, I will deliberate with my kinsmen." Wretched me, how nearly I promised! Wretched me, that I have only thirty days to be angry! Why do you wonder if you won over the other man more quickly? It is easier to forgive an injury than a crime. Come forward into the midst, old man, by whose mercy I am made cruel. "Now," he says, "the time is short — and have you leisure to prosecute?" Is this how a man wins another over? Is this how he pleads? It is plain that now for the first time you are asking. For what have I done like a madman? I have not been won over. The time has not yet passed; even now I can be won over. How unfair it is that I am not yet guilty and already a defendant!

The other side. Wretched me, father! Nothing has been taken from your anger, much from the time. I am more unfortunate than if I had won over neither. If you mean to save your son, there has already been time; if to kill him, there is time now. The man who was more feared was asked first.

4. The grandson got of a prostitute.
A certain man disowned his son. The disowned son betook himself to a prostitute and got a son by her. Falling ill, he sent for his father; when his father had come, he commended the boy to him and died. The father, after his son's death, took the grandson into adoption. He is accused by his other son of madness.

A new kind of madness is charged against me: I should have been sane, had I not acknowledged my own. I kept waiting for someone to plead for the disowned man: none of his kinsmen dared, since his brother held back. His failing breath was sustained until my coming. I entered; his eyes, already sinking, he raised at my name, and held back his fleeing spirit. Into my lap he laid both his son and his last breath. It was told me that my son was at the point of death — and not by his brother.

The other side. This boy's father is uncertain: it would go well with him, if his mother too were uncertain. Among his other misfortunes he fell in with a prostitute — and a fertile one. I do not know whether the woman did the more wrong against the father in taking from him an heir or in giving him one. He adopted the son of the very woman for whose sake he had cast out his own.

5. The wife tortured by the tyrant on her husband's behalf.
A wife, tortured by a tyrant as to whether she knew anything of her husband's plot against him, persisted in denying it. Afterwards her husband killed the tyrant. Within five years he divorced her, since she bore no child, on the ground of barrenness. She brings an action against him for ingratitude.

The marriage which the tyrant did not part, the tyrannicide has parted. Married women were dragged off, virgins were carried away; none then seemed more fortunate than those who had no children. The tyrant suspected this man of plotting his death, whether something slipped from him or his face did not well conceal great designs; yet he cannot complain of his wife's tongue, since he knows how she keeps silent. Set upon the rack, she looked back more often to her absent husband than to the tyrant before her eyes. The whole apparatus of tyrannic cruelty is unrolled against the unhappy woman, and those instruments that break the very spirits of men by the mere sight of them are set out to wring from her the knowledge in a woman's breast; her body is torn apart with stripes. I do not know, commonwealth, whether that woman will give you children; she gave you a tyrannicide. Do you wonder if five years passed between a tortured wife and a busy husband? Her body slit with whips, scorched with fire, racked with torments — you will pardon the woman, I think, if I say: she is weary. Why do you boast of tyrannicide? It is easier to kill a tyrant than to endure one. Whips, hot plates, the rack, whatever ancient savagery had devised, whatever the new age had added — what more shall I say? The tyrant tortured her even when he was inquiring about tyrannicide. Does she burden your purse, costly in her expenses, and, as the way of the age is — luxury flowing ever to the worse — does a woman's vanity rage in mutual rivalry to the point of public harm by private extravagance? Does she ask for gems and little stones sought from a foreign shore? Wait, she can yet bear a child; fertility does not answer to a fixed day. Nature is her own mistress. Which do you think the more to be wondered at — your tyrannicide or her silence?

The other side. "I was tortured." You would justly reproach me with it, had I not avenged you. Even if you knew of your husband's tyrannicide and did not betray it, it is no service not to commit a crime. And besides, you did not know; for I did not tell you, nor did I entrust so great a design — heavy even for the spirits of men — to a woman's chatter, which can keep silent only about what it does not know. At the time my wife was tortured I was thinking nothing yet of tyrannicide; afterwards I thought of it, and this very thing, the avenging of my wife, was my reason for thinking of it. If she kept silent about what she had heard, it is no service but mere good faith.

Outside. Lucius Vinicius, than whom no Roman citizen had a readier talent in pleading cases. Whatever long reflection was to furnish him, the first effort of his mind gave; he pleaded cases extempore, yet he did not desire this commendation — that he should seem to plead extempore. Of him the deified Augustus elegantly said: "Lucius Vinicius keeps his talent in ready cash."

6. The dissolute father and son.
A certain man, while his son lived in dissipation, began to live in dissipation himself. He is accused by his son of madness. The father speaks against it.

My accuser has within him conflicting feelings: he longs that the defendant be condemned and the charge acquitted. "But you are an old man," he says; this is what you mean: my dissipation began later and will end sooner. Some have said that the highest good is pleasure. I have no need of those who lay down precepts; I have an example. I have shown you the dissipation in yourself that you did not see in yourself. Drunk, you charge your father with drunkenness.

The other side. A young man who is dissolute sins; an old man who is dissolute is mad. No one imitates vices because he hates them. What general ever fled the battle himself, that his army might fight well? He does not check vices who provokes them. I too shall lay my own dissipation to my father's charge. I was not under a strict discipline, not under the rule of a well-ordered house, which might have formed a young man's character and led him away from the vices of his age. In a sense I was sent ahead to dissipation by my father. Grey hairs dripping with perfume, and an old reveller, are too dissolute for no one, but seem to no one quite sane.

7. The foreign trader.
A certain man who had a beautiful wife went abroad. A foreign trader moved into the woman's neighbourhood; three times he solicited her for sexual relations, raising his offers; she refused. The trader died; in his will he left the beautiful woman heir to all his goods, and added this notice: "because I found her chaste." She entered upon the inheritance. The husband returns and accuses her of adultery on suspicion.

Late is the complaint I bring: I do not accuse my wife of adultery until she is made rich. After such great profits of unchastity, if I can keep silent, I must confess that this was my reason for being away. It is time that a husband be believed concerning his wife. Let a married woman keep her eyes cast down to the ground, and toward an obliging caller be ungracious rather than immodest; let her refuse her unchastity by her looks far sooner than by her word. No one will ask again the woman who refuses with spirit. "Be sole heir of all my goods, because you could not be corrupted, because you so faithfully guarded your chastity." Pass over for a moment the name of the author: is it not the will of a husband that is believed? Has all the forbearance of our age now so departed that, against a husband's complaint, a wife is defended by another man's testimony? The foundation of women's vices is greed. She who can be without fear of the reputation of adultery, can be without fear of adultery. From every reef the purple-fish is gathered, with which the dress may be stained as with blood. Unhappy throngs of slave-girls labour, that the adulteress may be visible through a thin gown, and that a husband may know nothing more in his own wife's body than any stranger or foreigner. The old verdict I will assess by the future; meanwhile, what asks for her he found her — unchaste. All call you unchaste; chaste only one man, and a foreigner, who does more harm as praiser than as accuser. I never heard my wife called chaste except in the adulterer's notice. Cast your eyes to the ground and shut your ears to the voices of strangers: let each man refuse for himself on your behalf. He called her chaste, I call her unchaste: you will, I think, believe a citizen rather than a foreigner, a husband rather than an adulterer. The very notice he wrote with the mind of a seducer. "Because I found her chaste," he says — which befell no man but me.

The other side. She is beautiful: this was Nature's fault. She was without her husband: this was the husband's fault. She was solicited: this was another man's fault. She refused: this was chastely done. She was left an heir: this was good fortune. She entered upon the inheritance: this she did deliberately.

pr.1. I have known certain men, most eloquent, who did not answer to their reputation when they declaimed; speaking in the forum to the greatest admiration of all, the moment they withdrew to these domestic exercises they were deserted by their own talent. That this should happen to a good many is to me as strange as it is certain. And so I remember asking Cassius Severus what the reason was that in declamations his eloquence did not answer to him.

pr.2. For in no one did this happen more remarkably. His speech was vigorous, polished, full of mighty epigrams; no one allowed less of idleness in his pleading; there was no part that did not stand by its own merit, nothing in which a hearer could turn his mind elsewhere without loss, all of it intent, all aiming at some mark; no one held the feelings of his audience more in his own power. True is what our friend Gallio says of him: "When he spoke, he was master of the case, so completely did all do what he bade; when he wished it, they grew angry."

pr.3. "No one, while he spoke, but feared he would leave off." You must not judge him by what he published; there are indeed even these things by which his eloquence may be recognized; yet he was far greater heard than read. This did not happen to him in the proportion in which it happens to almost all to whom being heard is a greater recommendation than being read, but in him the difference is far greater. First, there was as much in the man as in the talent: a striking size of body, the sweetness of a most powerful voice — though these rarely come together, that the same voice be at once sweet and solid — a delivery such as could have produced an actor, and yet not such as could seem an actor's.

pr.4. For there was nothing you would wonder at in him more than that the gravity which was wanting to his life was overflowing in his pleading: so long as he kept himself short of jests, his speech was that of a censor. Then, the very things he spoke were better than what he wrote. For being a man of ready presence of mind, and of greater talent than application, he pleased more in the things he discovered than in the things he had brought prepared. And indeed when angry he spoke better, and so men took the most careful precaution not to interrupt him while speaking.

pr.5. He alone profited by being caught off guard; fortune always deserved better of him than care. Yet this good luck never persuaded him to negligence. In one day he would plead several private cases, and so as to plead one before noon, another after; but a public case never more than one in a day. And yet I do not know of any defendant he undertook except himself: so completely did he find nowhere any subject for speaking except in his own perils.

pr.6. He never spoke without notes, nor was he content with that kind of notes in which the bare facts are set down, but for the most part the pleading was written out in full; even those things that could be said wittily were jotted down; but though he would not come forward unless equipped, he gladly fell away from his apparatus. Forced to speak extempore, he outran himself beyond measure. It was always more useful for him to be caught out than to be prepared; but you would admire him the more for not abandoning his diligence, since rashness served him so well.

pr.7. He had, then, everything that might equip him to declaim well: a diction not common nor sordid, but choice; a manner of speaking not slack or languid, but ardent and impetuous; explanations not slow nor empty, but holding more of thought than of words; diligence, the greatest support even of a middling talent. Yet when he declaimed he was not only far below himself, but below many: and so he rarely declaimed, and not unless forced by friends.

pr.8. But when I asked why in declamations he was unequal to himself, he would say this: "What you wonder at in me happens to nearly all. Even great talents — from which I know I am far removed — when have they excelled in more than one work? Cicero's eloquence forsook him in his verses; that felicity of talent left Vergil in unfettered prose; Sallust's speeches are read for the honour of his histories; the speech of the most eloquent man, Plato, which was written for Socrates, is worthy neither of the advocate nor of the defendant.

pr.9. "This you may see happen not only to talents but to bodies, whose strengths are not suited to all that is done by strength: with this one no one is a match in wrestling; that one is mighty to lift a load of great weight; that one, whatever he grasps, does not let go, but lays his hands, that will hold them back, on vehicles thrusting downhill. I come to animals: some hounds are bred for the boar, some for the stag; the swiftness of horses, though they be very fast, is not fitted for the racecourse in all; some better endure a rider, some the yoke.

pr.10. "To call you to my own malady: Pylades in comedy, Bathyllus in tragedy, fell far short of themselves; to my namesake, since swiftness of foot is not only not conceded but cast in his teeth, the hands are slower; some fight best against the heavy-armed, some against the Thracians, and some so desire to be matched with a left-handed man as . . . In oratory itself, although the subject be one, yet he who argues best narrates more carelessly; that one does not fill out so well as he prepares. Our friend Passienus, when he begins to speak — straight after his exordium there is a general flight; for the epilogue we all return; only those who must, hear the middle parts.

pr.11. "Do you wonder that the same man does not declaim as well as he pleads cases, or that the same man does not speak deliberative themes so well as forensic ones? Pompeius Silo, seated, is both fluent and learned, and would be reckoned eloquent if he would dismiss us after his preface: he declaims so badly that I seem to have wished him well when I said, 'May you never rise.' A great and varied thing is eloquence, and it has not yet so indulged anyone as to fall to him whole; he is fortunate enough who has been admitted to some part of it.

pr.12. "I, however, seem able also to give my own reason: I have grown accustomed to look not at a hearer but at a judge; I have grown accustomed not to answer myself but my opponent; I avoid saying superfluous things no less than contradictory ones. In a school-piece what is not superfluous, when the thing itself is superfluous? I will show you my feeling: when I speak in the forum, I am doing something; when I declaim, it is, as Censorinus very prettily used to say of those who ambitiously sought offices in country towns: I seem to myself to be labouring in a dream. Then the very thing is different:

pr.13. "it is one thing entirely to fight, another to flourish weapons in the air. The school has always been so reckoned to be a kind of training-ground, the forum the arena; and that is why a man about to speak for the first time in the forum is called a raw recruit. Come now, lead those declaimers into the senate, into the forum: they will be changed along with the place; like bodies accustomed to a closed room and a pampering shade, they cannot stand in the open, they do not know how to bear rain or sun, they will scarcely find themselves; for they have grown used to being eloquent at their own pleasure.

pr.14. "You must not look for an orator in this boyish exercise. What if you should wish to judge a helmsman in a fish-pond? I would excuse myself to you more carefully, as if I were not born for this thing, did I not know that both Asinius Pollio and Messala Corvinus and Passienus, who now stands in the first rank, are less well received than Cestius or Latro.

pr.15. "Which, then, do you think is the fault — of those who speak or of those who hear? They do not speak worse, but these judge with worse taste, who, being mostly boys or youths, frequent the schools; these not only prefer their Cestius to the most eloquent men I mentioned a little while ago, but would prefer him even to Cicero, if they did not fear stones. Yet in the one way they can, they do prefer him: for they learn this man's declamations by heart, and read that man's speeches only those to which Cestius wrote replies.

pr.16. "I remember entering his school when he was about to recite his speech against Milo; Cestius, after his custom, said in self-admiration: 'If I were a Thracian, I would be Fusius; if I were a pantomime, I would be Bathyllus; if a horse, Melissio.' I could not contain my bile and cried out: 'If you were a sewer, you would be the Great Sewer.' Huge was the laughter of all; the schoolmen stared at me, asking who I was that had so thick a neck. Cestius, about to reply to Cicero, found nothing to answer me, but said he would not go on unless I left the house.

pr.17. "I said I would not leave a public bath until I had bathed. Then it pleased me to give Cestius satisfaction concerning Cicero in the forum. Catching him soon after, I summon him to law before the praetor, and when I had poured out as much jesting and abuse as I wished, I demanded that the praetor admit his name under the law concerning recorded wrongdoing. So great was his confusion that he asked for an adjournment. Then I brought him before another praetor and prosecuted him for ingratitude. Now before the city praetor I was asking that a guardian be appointed for him; when friends intervened — they had run together for this spectacle — and entreated me, I said I would trouble him no further if he would swear that Cicero was more eloquent than himself. And not by jest nor in earnest could he be brought to do this."

pr.18. "I have told you this little tale," he said, "that you might know that in declamations there is almost another race of men. If I wish to be compared with them, I need not a greater talent, but a smaller taste." And so it could scarcely now be obtained of him that he should declaim; and this could not be obtained at all — that he should be willing to have any hearers but his most intimate friends. And so he did. His declamations were unequal, but those passages that stood out, if you had set them in any declamation whatever, would have made it unequal: a rough arrangement, and one that avoided arrangement, but living epigrams. It will, however, be unfair to judge him by what I shall presently add; for these are not the things he said best, but the things I best remember.

1. The spendthrift blinded by his fellows.
Let a blind man receive a thousand denarii from the public funds. Ten young men, when they had eaten up their goods, drew lots, so that the one whose name came out should, by their compact, be blinded and so receive a thousand denarii. The lot of one of them came out; he was blinded. He asks for the thousand denarii. They are refused.

These are the eyes you feared, husbands. O for a law to be repealed, if it blinds men! The commonwealth gives a thousand denarii to no one but him who receives it unwillingly. Say now, "have pity"; this you did not say when you were being blinded. The commonwealth consoles infirmity; it does not buy it. Their patrimonies consumed, they bring in their limbs. It is more useful to the commonwealth that one blind man be turned away than that nine more be made. He does not ask support of you alone, but first of many. I will support the man who is supported because of his infirmity; I will not support the man who is made infirm for the sake of support. So it falls out, when men spend the greater part of their lives in darkness, that at last they loathe the sun as superfluous.

The other side. He will give nothing to those nine: he will be in nobody's favour, if he cheats the men by whom he was blinded . . . The young man, encircled by those nine veteran spendthrifts, says: "Alone, I could not resist nine in agreement." It was all done by arrangement: one made the proposal, all approved it; one was chosen to draw the lots; his lot was put in to come out first. When he resisted, he was blinded. "If he was encircled," he says, "let him pursue the wrong, let him sue for violence, let him seek redress in kind." We shall see; the first thing is that he have something to live on.

2. The parricide acquitted by an even vote.
A certain man accused his son of parricide. When the son was acquitted by an even vote, he disowns him.

What I now ask is less; I do not seek that you avenge me against a parricide, but that you separate me from him. I do not accuse the parricide, I flee from him. When will this man spare an accuser, who did not spare a father? Is there, then, nothing between the will and the sack? Not an acquitted parricide, but a doubtful one: to be acquitted you need many votes; to be condemned, one. They did not acquit the defendant, but spared the age. Do you wonder at mercy in a city in which the law grants acquittal even on equal tablets? Do you ask by how many you are disapproved? If I add one, you are a parricide. You owe your acquittal to the law, not to your innocence. "I was acquitted," he says. I do not disown you for parricide, but for other vices that made you so credible a parricide.
The other side. The young man's colour is plain: that he should say he was overborne by his father's authority.

3. The man to be disowned who adopted his disowned brother.
Let a father divide the patrimony with a son in his thirtieth year. A certain man had a thrifty son and a dissolute one. He disowned the dissolute one. The thrifty one set out abroad; he was captured by pirates; he wrote to his father about his ransom. While the father held back, the dissolute son forestalled him and ransomed his brother. The thrifty son returned; he adopted his brother. He is disowned.

There is no reason for anyone to praise me: my brother first set between us the example of family devotion; together he sailed, together he ran the risk, together he traversed every land, leaving me only at our father's house. There is no reason for you to use the excuse of age: you can sail. He ought to give thanks to us both: my brother brought me back to this man, I brought this man his brother. If you disowned him as a sluggard, he has sailed; if as undutiful, he has ransomed his own. What a son has received from the law cannot be snatched from him; for how can a father snatch away what he cannot but give?

The other side. Through the one I am compelled to disown the one I do not wish to. In this one thing the two please each other: that each displeases his father. Let us use the medicine to which we are driven, as is wont to be done with dangerous wounds — that the evil be cut out along with the body itself. Do you permit a young man to adopt, whom the law tests in the dividing of a patrimony? The law admitted you to the service of the patrimony, not to its ownership. Is there any age at which a man ceases to be a son? Not even to a thirty-year-old son is it permitted to adopt; for no one can take another into his own power who is himself in another's power. How can it be that you have the power of life and death over a brother, but not over a son? If he had deserved well of you, you would have begged your father on your brother's behalf. For that I did not ransom him was a matter of poverty: nothing was left in the common store; whatever the thirty-year-old had left, the disowned son had carried off. What was I to do, alone, an old man, helpless, whose patrimony one had divided and the other consumed?

4. Saved by his son.
Let one who has been saved have no right of action against his saviour. A father who has been saved by his son disowns him. The son enters a plea in bar.

I might have been allowed to perish, if I am not allowed to speak. Do you think me saved? I was taken captive. Give me back to the enemy; captives are allowed to speak. Since he boasts so greatly of the gift of life, hear who gave it first. If anyone gives me back to the enemy, I will call him my saviour. Or do you think disowning an action at law? Even if it is an action, the law that speaks of one saved pertains only to outside persons, to son and father no more than to slave and master, freedman and patron. To depart from a father's power and come to the assessment of the favour: he who gives life, if he first received it, does not bind, but repays. I went into the battle line as an example to my son; not the enemy but age conquered me; he saved the one who had often saved him. A prostitute calls me an old man come back to life, I am matter for the jests of parasites; by all of them, as if they were my saviours, I am bidden to keep silent. Son, if I am not allowed to live, why was I not allowed to perish? "I shielded you," he says. So you, a young man, did not stand before your father in the line? Hear my son's glory: he did not commit parricide; when he could have saved me, he saved me.
The other side. This man begot me; he gave me my breath, he gave me these hands by which he was to be saved.

5. The father who keeps back the ravished woman.
Let a ravished woman choose either the death of her ravisher or marriage without a dowry. The ravisher demands that the ravished woman be brought forth. Her father is unwilling.

He is the ravisher, and I am hauled into court. It is not so easy for an honest man to kill as for a desperate one to die. "The law," he says, "is common to both." May the gods grant that you do not force me to try whether all of it is mine. "When, then," he says, "will she make her choice?" At this time she cannot; I am tending her wounds, I am restoring my household, I am mourning my stormed house, I am consoling her ravished virginity, I am guarding one who threatens her own life. When will she choose? When the ravished woman wishes, not when the ravisher. When will she choose? When you do not wish it. "When," he says, "will she choose?" I am preparing myself for the choice, I am steeling my mind; it is not easy to kill a man; meanwhile I press down my groans and drive inward the tears that burst forth. You know what will happen: my face has deceived you. Fool, do you think anyone delays his daughter's marriage? You run upon the axe and call the executioner of your own accord. When you ought to be begging, you offer insult. No one is compelled to avenge himself.

The other side. Nothing is more wretched than to be left in doubt between life and death. It will now be a kindness, even if she chooses death. I fell in love with this man's daughter. I should have approached the father about marriage; I did so; but you see how, even in respect of the law, he is slow. The ravisher has his life at another's discretion, his liberty at his own. This law is common to both. This ravisher has something to fear, and something too that he may hope for. "In the law," he says, "it is not written when." Nay, at once; whenever a time is not added, the present is understood. Shall so long a right over a citizen's life be permitted you? It is crueller than to die — always to fear death.

6. The house burned along with the tyrant.
Let there be an action for damage done. A certain man, while pursuing a tyrant who was fleeing from the citadel, drove him into a private house. He set fire to the house: the tyrant was burned up along with the house. He received a reward. The owner sues him for the damage.

Whom did you shut out and whom did you take in? Why did the tyrant make for no other house? Everyone shut his house against him as he came. I had no entrance into the house, who had one into the citadel. Do you not rejoice to have spent something on the public liberty? "This is the man in whose house the tyrant was killed." You are pointed out as a tyrannicide. "Give me back my house," he says. So while the tyrant lived you had not lost it? The tyrant's friend, the tyrant's henchman, certainly — what you cannot deny — his host. Long I waited to see whether the tyrant would be cast out. You can more easily accuse either yourself, who were so intimate with the tyrant that your house most of all pleased him, who took him in; or the tyrant, who did you the damage in fleeing into your house; or, that I may free you from blame, you can more easily accuse fortune, which brought the tyrant to you of all men.

The other side. The damage ought to be his whose the reward is. It is not unfair that the wrong of that thing be charged to you, the fruit of which you have reaped. The tyrant did not choose the house — for he had no leisure for that — but burst into the one he could, when I was not in it. This man, having found an occasion of doing harm, would not enter, but chose a tyrannicide that was doubtful, slow, dangerous to the city. He received a reward, no doubt the greater, as if he ought to make good the damage.

7. Poison given to a frenzied son.
A father gave poison to his son, who was frenzied and tearing his own limbs. He is accused by his wife of ill-treatment.
It is no wonder why she lives who has lost her son: he lives who killed him.
The other side. The one I was losing every day, I at last buried. You are mistaken, unhappy woman, as to the time of your bereavement: not then did you lose your son, but then you buried him.

Outside. Alfius Flavus spoke this epigram: "He was himself both his own nourishment and his own undoing." Cestius, rebuking him as though he had spoken with a corrupt taste, said: "It is plain that you read the poets eagerly: that thought is his who has filled this age not only with amatory arts but with amatory epigrams. For Ovid in his books of Metamorphoses says:
'He himself began to rend his own limbs with mangling bite,
and the unhappy man fed his body by diminishing it.'"

8. The Olynthian father charged with assembling a mob.
Let one who has made a gathering and an assembly be liable to capital punishment. When Olynthus was conquered, an old Olynthian came with his young son to Athens. The Athenians decreed citizenship to all the Olynthians. Invited to dinner by a dissolute young man, he came with his son. There, when there was mention of debauching the son, the father fled, and the young man was held back. The father began to weep before the house; the house was set on fire; ten young men perished, and the Olynthian's son. The father is accused of having made a gathering and an assembly.

If a wretched man is not allowed to weep, he must weep the more. Silence cannot be commanded to grief. There were men among the people who said: "Here he debauched my son, here my wife"; each man brought there both his own fire and his own grief. I fear, my son, that while I seek you I may fall upon the bones of some ravisher. Where is the good faith of Athens? Where are the hospitable hands joined on either side? "We are taken captive, my son," I said; "while we may, let us flee — but as from Philip. At least in Philip's hands we were men together." My tears are turned into a charge, as though from the time Olynthus was taken I had ceased to weep. So great, forsooth, am I, that I could rouse the people in a city in which I could not save my son. It is not, whenever several have come together to some place, a gathering and an assembly, but whenever men have been called together, whenever, prepared as if to their leader, they have run together; not if one neighbourhood has met, or the number of a few passers-by has flowed in, but where the whole people, or the greater part of it, where the city has been divided into parties. A gathering is the name for a great multitude coming together by some common agreement: but there at the start there were few, and then the rest came together not to me, but to the fire — which, even so, the people chose to watch rather than put out. The law punishes not the man on whose account a gathering was made, but the man by whom it was made. Vengeance was not so dear to me that I should be willing to lose my son; and I tried to beg the people, and could not.
The other side. What need of a gathering? There are laws written for the avenging of all wrongs. Once stirred, a multitude keeps no measure. The city might have burned in that fire.

9. The crucifixion of the slave who refused his master poison.
A master, being ill, asked his slave to give him poison. He did not give it. He provided in his will that the slave be crucified by the heirs. The slave appeals to the tribunes.

Cornelian law, I call upon you; behold, my master commands what you forbid. That no one may think he had displeased his master, he ordered the cross prepared for him at the same time as the poison for himself. We confess more crimes of the slave: he refused his master, when he wanted them, untimely draughts and harmful foods. For what did he not want, who asked for poison? He chose to suffer the cross rather than to deserve it. If he loses, he is to die; if he does not lose, he is to be the slave of the man by whom he is demanded for the cross. On one side is the law, on the other the will, and on both sides the cross. The madman wanted to kill his slave without cause. Do you seek a proof of his madness? He wanted to kill himself too. "The tribunes," he says, "cannot help a slave." A slave's son we had for a king; by a slave's information the conspiracy of Brutus's sons with the Tarquins was laid bare. Is there, then, no difference whether a man gave his master poison or refused it? Even where to die is a remedy, to kill is a crime. Do you wish a slave to despair of his master's life as quickly as an heir does? If you think death a punishment, why do you ask for it? If a benefit, why do you threaten it? Does anyone reproach a man with poison except given poison? Will you set any limit to the tribunician power, which the Roman people, that it might itself have the most power, willed to be stronger than itself? To have poison is a crime as great as to kill one's master.

The other side. Wishing to die, he chose for this service the most worthless slave, a bold one, one hostile to him. He took thought not for his master's safety, whom he saw wasting away with an incurable disease, but prolonged his torments. A slave is not the censor of his master's command, but its minister. The right of wills is at stake, all the power of which has perished, if slaves disregard the commands of the living and become tribunes of the dead. So then, you gallows-bird, you will not die at your master's pleasure, but your master will die at yours?

1. The bond with the disowned son.
A brother gave his disowned brother a bond promising to give him half the inheritance if he did not speak against it. The disowned man kept silent. The other is disowned by the father.

He has as much debt as he could not pay while his father lives. Do you wish to know what your credit is worth? Not even your brother trusted you without a bond. The one I delay in his hope, the other in his good faith. I am alive, and already my patrimony has been divided. Unless you help me, even the man who kept silent will defeat me. I do not conceal that today I am disowning two. Bring out the bond, the compact of parricides and the pact of unholy hope, the bond impious in the giver, base in the receiver, dangerous to the father.

The other side. In every fortune, brother, I will join myself to you as your companion: if there is soldiering to do, we will soldier together; if travel abroad, together we will wander through cities; if I beg my daily alms, even that I will share with you. I did not wish my father's fresh anger to be stirred up; I preferred that, by keeping silent, he should overcome our father. I will be heir of my own portion, guardian of yours. And because in the greatest matters each man trusts himself best, I give the bond; do you take care to seem to receive that portion rather from your father than from your brother. This thing which we were doing honourably and dutifully, we did so openly that our father knew it. For what did I fear? That, if my father learned of it, he would take it ill that his son is no greedy man, that his brother is dutiful? So may it fall to me that my father be reconciled to us both.

2. The exiled father barred by the country-house.
Let it not be lawful to help an exile with shelter and food. Let one condemned for unintentional homicide be exiled for five years. A certain man, who had a son and a daughter, condemned for unintentional homicide, set out into exile and used to come to an estate that bordered on his own. The son learned of this and beat the overseer; the overseer shut the father out. He began to go to his daughter. She, accused of having received an exile, was acquitted with her brother as advocate. After five years the father disowns the son.

The accuser made me an exile from my city, the son from my own people too. I found my daughter more honourable, in that she was accused; my slave more thrifty, in that he was beaten. You deserved ill of your father, whom you shut out; of your sister, whom you harmed by a precedent; of the judges, whom you feared in so good a cause. Either you did wrong, or your sister. My own son taught me, in that I do not receive him. "My sister," he says, "was acquitted with me as advocate." So you would not receive your father, when you could plead this cause so well? When the woman who had received him was acquitted, the man who had driven him out was condemned. My daughter judged me her father, my slaves their master; to my son alone I was an exile. Forgive me, most faithful of little slaves, I unwittingly harmed you too. How good do you think that cause was, which was not condemned even with you as advocate? If I can die with you as my heir, I am worthy to leave you even this slave. To another he is an exile, to you he is a father. No law commands a crime. At least she who did it was acquitted. The law holds the man who helped an exile, not the one who suffers him to be helped. Be ignorant, pretend not to see: the law bids you be innocent, not inquisitive. If you were doing it for my sake, you would have warned me, you would have barred the slave, you would not have beaten him.

The other side. I could not act when the law forbade. She was accused and acquitted, because she seemed a poor woman who did not know the laws. I feared not for myself but for you: the matter had come to men's knowledge; you were being hunted; I feared you would be killed. Do you wish to know it was known? My sister was accused. I chose to beat a most thrifty slave rather than to lose the best of fathers.

3. The mother of the bastard chosen as a portion.
Let the elder brother divide the patrimony, the younger choose. Let it be lawful to rear a son by a slave-woman. A certain man, who had a legitimate son, reared another by a slave-woman, and died. The elder brother divided thus, that he set the whole patrimony on one side, and on the other the mother of the bastard. The younger chose the mother and accuses his brother of fraud.

I alone of all men have been disinherited by the dividing. "He should have chosen the other portion," he says. You alone could be such a son as you are a brother. The law bade you divide, me choose: openly it fears lest the younger be defrauded. He divided thus, that, if I did not wish to be a beggar, I should leave my brother in want and my mother in slavery. It is not dividing, to set the patrimony on one side and a burden on the other. He was such a son that his father reared a co-heir for him by a slave-woman. Choose, so as to lack either the patrimony or the crime. Those are wont to be called defrauders who have carried something off: this man left nothing. "You yourself," he says, "wished to be poor." Why then do I complain, if I delight in want? "What was done by law," he says, "cannot be charged." Nay, nothing can be charged except what was done by law; for if anything was otherwise done, it is of itself void. Fraud always wraps a crime under the appearance of law: what is apparent in it is lawful, what lies hidden is insidious. Fraud always reaches injury through right. The law bids the elder divide, the younger choose: you did not divide, nor did this man choose; he was so bound by you that he must needs prefer what did not profit him. My devotion toward my mother was known; he did not fear that I could choose the other portion.

The other side. I did nothing but divide. The fraud is not in the division, but in the choosing. You have a mother whom some have ransomed with their whole goods; you have a glory that some have sought through fire, through arms. She carried off much of the patrimony, having, by a slave-woman's effrontery, the right of a mistress. Did you fear I would rage against her? It did not profit me, since in her I was about to have the whole patrimony. As it is, you have just as much; for you have the portion you wished. That you should have just as much, not even your father had wished; therefore he left your mother a slave.

4. The drink deadly in part.
Let there be an action for poisoning. A wife followed her proscribed husband. At a certain time she asked him, as he held a cup in secret, what it was; he said poison, and that he wished to die. She asked him to give her a share, and said she did not wish to live without him. He drank part himself, gave part to his wife. She alone perished. By the will the husband was found heir. Restored, he is charged with poisoning.

He acted so as to be caught, was caught so as to be entreated, drank so as to live. What is this poison that harms only the heir? No one ever gave his wife poison so openly. He flees being killed, who says he longs to die. One man has been made richer by the proscription. To make him wish to live, his wife could not persuade him; a more alluring thing persuaded him, his wife's inheritance. He knew which part of the draught he was draining. The opposing party he pursued with the sword, his own with poison. The conquerors made an end of killing sooner than the conquered. What did you suppose would happen, when the wife had carried a will into exile, and the husband poison? Where is the wife? Are you not ashamed? Now even the proscribed return. As soon as she took the draught, she collapsed. Do not wonder if the poison is so effective: he is heir who gave it. Generally a light and harmless fluid hangs at the top, while that heavy and deadly part sinks by its own weight. It is plain that you had long had the poison prepared: you knew how to divide it. Even if one who gave it to a willing woman can be defended, can you, who made her willing? It was the kind of poison that, by its weight, sank to the bottom of the draught. This man drank as far as the poison, his wife drank the poison.

The other side. She loved her husband in peace, followed him in war, did not abandon him in his last counsel. O a woman worthy that I, innocent, should follow her! I waged civil war, I was proscribed, I went into exile; what can be added to these ills, except that I should drink poison and live? "It is poison," I said. Those who mean to give poison conceal it. Cato sold poison. Ask whether it was lawful for a proscribed man to buy what it was lawful for Cato to sell.

5. Iphicrates as defendant.
Let one who has done violence in a trial be punished with death. Iphicrates, sent against the king of the Thracians, twice conquered in the line, struck a treaty with him and married his daughter. When he had returned to Athens and was pleading his cause, certain men in Thracian dress were seen, armed, around the court, and the defendant himself drew his sword. When the judges were summoned to give judgement, they openly cast votes of acquittal. He is accused of having done violence in the trial.

Not one of your judges but feared as though you were going to judge them. He came as advocate with his whole kingdom; he did not array his war with greater forces than his trial. Iphicrates, sheathe your sword; it is a trial. What have you to do with a sword? Surely those twice conquered must lay down their arms. What is this exchange against the nature of things — a wedding in war, a war in a trial?

The other side. I did no violence; for all the lawful forms were carried out: the accuser spoke in his place, the defendant answered in his; the trial was completed in all its parts. While the judges were casting their votes, I drew my sword, to kill myself if I were condemned. The judges cast their votes of acquittal openly, to return thanks to their general. The reason for the marriage was the advantage of the commonwealth. The soldier had rather often been beaten in an unlucky battle. The barbarians around the court were armed not for any service, but after their own custom. "What," he says, "can you complain of? That I brought you a hostage?"

6. The adulteress and poisoner.
Let there be an action for poisoning. A certain man who had a wife and by her a marriageable daughter told his wife to whom he meant to give her in marriage. She said: "She will die sooner than marry that man." The girl died before her wedding day, with doubtful signs of indigestion and of poison. The father tortured a slave-girl; she said she knew nothing of poison, but knew of an adultery between her mistress and the man to whom he meant to give the daughter. He accuses his wife of poisoning and adultery.

"She will die" — I have the poisoner; "sooner than marry" — I have the adulteress. "She will die" — it was done; "sooner than marry" — it was done. The adultery I detected later than it was done, the poisoning before it was done. Two crimes I have brought before you, and two informers: one tells what has been done, the other even what is to come. To her son-in-law an adulteress, to her daughter a rival. How unhappy is the house in which adultery is the proof! I said, "He is honourable"; I said, "He is handsome"; while I praised the son-in-law, I recommended the adulterer. O how slow I am in my own misfortunes! The poisoning, even when foretold, I did not believe; the adultery I detected only in the poisoning. The wedding was turned into a funeral, the marriage-bed changed into a bier, the happy torches set beneath the pyre. The body is brought forth, rotting and swollen with poisons. What more do you ask? The signs agree with the words, the tortures with the signs. The deeds agree with your voice. "She will die before she marries" — it was done. We saw the flowing body, and in her corpse we believed the mother's words. I lost my son-in-law by adultery, my wife by parricide, my daughter by poisoning.

The other side. He has charged two most grievous crimes, adultery and poisoning: the adultery on a slave-girl's testimony, the poisoning not even on a slave-girl's. When she was indignant at not being consulted, words slipped from her — words of one who mourns her daughter no less than he does. But why did you say, "She will die sooner than marry that man"? Words slipped out, too little considered in grief. And very often divination is fortuitous.

7. The madman who gave up his wife to his son.
Let there be an action for madness. A man who had two sons married a wife. One of the young men, when he was ill and at the last, the physicians said had a sickness of the mind. The father entered to his son with drawn sword, and asked him to tell him the cause. He said he was in love with his stepmother. The father gave up his wife to him. He is accused by the other son of madness.

Hear a new thing: a cruel brother, a merciful stepmother. I am mad, because by my kindness someone is well. I handed over my wife to him; but I had snatched her away. "I call to witness," he said, "the gods who watch over filial love: I began to love her before you married her." So you call it an injury, that you have a brother and have not a stepmother? I passed before this man's eyes with a blade; no one but a sick man wrested the sword from me. To a father who could not endure the danger of a dying son, pardon must be given in whatever deed.

The other side. One was cured by pandering, the other recovered by parricide. What? Do you not think that adultery, which is committed with the husband bringing it about? I do not know whether he married more madly, or kept her, or dismissed her, or gave her away. How mad is the man to whom adultery is reckoned as a kindness! The husband drew his sword, not to avenge adultery, but to bring it about. The brother ought rather to have died than to be healed disgracefully. For what if he had coveted his mother, his sister? Some remedies are graver than the dangers themselves. Everything was contrived between stepson and stepmother; a sickness was feigned, and a father mocked by the basest of mimes.

8. The verse of the Vestal Virgin.
A Vestal Virgin wrote this verse:
"Happy the wedded! May I die if marriage is not sweet."
She is charged with unchastity. "Happy the wedded" — this is the word of one who longs for it; "may I perish if" — this is the word of one who affirms; "marriage is sweet" — either you swear from experience or you forswear from inexperience; neither befits a priestess. To you the magistrates lower their fasces, to you the consuls and praetors yield the road; are you a virgin for so paltry a reward? Let a priestess swear rarely, and never except by her own Vesta. "May I die" — has the eternal fire been put out? "May I die" — have you been approached about marriage? You at last, Vesta, I invoke, that you be as hostile to your priestess as you are hateful to her. Recite the verse, while I ask what kind it is. Would you write verse, would you soften words to your own measures, and break by melody the severity owed to the temple? But if you must needs praise marriage, tell of Lucretia, write of her death before you swear about your own. O you, worthy of every punishment, to whom anything is happier than the priesthood! "It is sweet" — how vivid a word, how sent up from the depths of the heart, not only of one who has experienced it but of one who has delighted in it. Even without defilement, she who longs for defilement is unchaste.

The other side. One verse is charged against her, and not even this one whole. "She ought not," he says, "to write verse." It is a great difference whether you rebuke or punish. No one can be condemned for unchastity but a woman whose body has been violated. What? Do you think that poets write what they feel? She lived modestly, with restraint; her dress was not too luxurious, her converse with men not too free; I confess to you her one crime: she has talent. Why should she not envy Cornelia? Why not the woman who bore Cato?
Outside. Varius Geminus said before Caesar: "Caesar, those who dare to speak before you are ignorant of your greatness; those who do not dare, of your humanity."
